lead: HDLC and PPP give reliable point‑to‑point links. They wrap user data in a flag‑delimited frame, add an address, a control field and a 16‑bit CRC. The same framing is reused in PPP, which adds a negotiation phase (LCP) so that two ends can agree on authentication, compression and network‑layer protocol. These protocols are used on serial links, DSL modems, and in many WAN routers.
prereq: You need: Framing and bit stuffing, Error detection: CRC‑16.

blocks.text: An HDLC frame starts and ends with the flag pattern 01111110 (hex 0x7E). Between the flags the sender places an address byte, a control byte, the payload data and a 16‑bit Frame Check Sequence (FCS). The FCS is the CRC‑16 computed over address, control and data. After the FCS the closing flag is sent.

items: Transmit flag 0x7E.
Transmit address byte.
Transmit control byte.
Transmit data bytes.
Compute CRC‑16 over address, control and data; append low‑order byte first.
Transmit closing flag 0x7E.
Bit stuffing: after five consecutive 1 bits the transmitter inserts a 0 to avoid creating a false flag.
The receiver removes any stuffed 0 after five 1s before CRC checking.

blocks.text: FCS = CRC‑16(poly=0x8005, init=0xFFFF, refIn=true, refOut=true, xorOut=0x0000)
blocks.where: FCS is a 16‑bit value; poly is the generator polynomial; init is the initial register; refIn/Out indicate bit reflection.

blocks.text: HDLC defines three link modes. In Normal Response Mode (NRM) the secondary may transmit only after receiving a Set‑Asynchronous‑Balanced‑Mode (SABM) from the primary. Asynchronous Balanced Mode (ABM) allows both ends to send frames whenever they have data, using a simple “I‑frame” for information and “RR”/“REJ” for flow control. Extended Asynchronous Balanced Mode (EABM) adds larger sequence numbers, so the window can be up to 127 frames.

items: NRM is used on legacy leased lines where one side is a master.
ABM is the default for modern PPP links.
EABM is useful when high‑speed links need a larger sliding window.
Primary sends SABM → secondary replies with UA (Unnumbered Acknowledgement).
Both sides may now exchange I‑frames.
If a frame is lost, the receiver sends REJ; the sender retransmits from the rejected sequence number.

blocks.text: PPP reuses the HDLC flag 0x7E and the same CRC‑16. The PPP frame adds a two‑byte Protocol field after the address (0xFF) and control (0x03) bytes. The Protocol field identifies the network‑layer protocol, e.g., 0x0021 for IPv4. Before data exchange the two ends run Link Control Protocol (LCP) to negotiate options such as authentication (PAP/CHAP), compression and the maximum receive unit (MRU).

items: Send LCP Configure‑Request with desired options.
Receive LCP Configure‑Ack, Configure‑Nak or Configure‑Reject.
Repeat until both sides acknowledge the same set of options.
Open the network‑layer protocol (e.g., IPCP for IPv4).
PPP is defined in RFC 1661 (and subsequently in ISO/IEC 1172).
Because PPP uses HDLC framing, any device that can decode HDLC can also decode PPP.

examples.question: A point‑to‑point link uses HDLC. The address byte is 0xFF, the control byte is 0x03 and the payload is one data byte 0xAB. Compute the CRC‑16 (poly 0x8005, init 0xFFFF, reflected) and write the complete bit sequence transmitted, including bit‑stuffing if needed.
steps: Bytes to be protected: FF, 03, AB.
Frame before stuffing: 7E FF 03 AB 00 BF 7E.
Apply bit‑stuffing after the opening flag: after five consecutive 1s insert a 0.
Final transmitted bit sequence (MSB first, with stuffing):
examples.answer: The CRC‑16 is 0xBF00 and the transmitted bit sequence (with stuffing) is shown above.

traps: Confusing the HDLC flag 0x7E with the PPP Protocol field; the flag is always 0x7E, the Protocol field follows address and control.
Applying bit stuffing before appending the CRC; stuffing must be done after the CRC is added, otherwise the receiver will mis‑detect the flag.
Using the non‑reflected CRC‑16 (poly 0x1021) instead of the reflected version required by HDLC, which yields a different FCS.
Writing the CRC low‑order byte first but then transmitting it in big‑endian order; the correct order for HDLC is low byte first.

quiz.q: What is the hexadecimal value of the HDLC flag byte?
In PPP, what two‑byte Protocol field value identifies IPv4?
Why does HDLC perform bit stuffing after the CRC‑16 (FCS) is appended to the frame?
quiz.a: Bit stuffing prevents the accidental appearance of the flag pattern 01111110 inside the transmitted bits, including the CRC. By inserting a 0 after any sequence of five consecutive 1s, the receiver can reliably detect the start and end of a frame and will not mistake data or CRC bits for a flag.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the Link Control Protocol (LCP) phase in PPP?
quiz.a: LCP negotiates link‑level options before user data is exchanged. It allows the two ends to agree on authentication method, compression, maximum receive unit (MRU) and other parameters, ensuring both sides operate with compatible settings.

quiz.q: Given address 0x01, control 0x02 and data bytes 0xAA 0x55, compute the reflected CRC‑16 used by HDLC and write the complete HDLC frame in hexadecimal (include flag and CRC). List the key steps.
quiz.a: Steps: 1) Form the byte sequence to protect: 01 02 AA 55. 2) Initialise CRC register to 0xFFFF. 3) Process each byte with the reflected polynomial 0x8005 (implementation shown in chapter). 4) After processing all bytes the CRC value is 0x4707. 5) Append CRC low‑order byte first: 07 47. 6) Add opening and closing flags 0x7E. Final frame: 7E 01 02 AA 55 07 47 7E.

quiz.q: A PPP link uses address 0xFF, control 0x03, Protocol 0x0021 (IPv4) and payload bytes 0x45 0x00. Compute the HDLC‑style CRC‑16 and write the full PPP frame in hex, showing flag, address, control, protocol, payload, CRC and closing flag.
quiz.a: Steps: 1) Bytes to protect: FF 03 21 45 00 (Protocol field is two bytes 0x00 0x21, transmitted low‑order first as 0x21 0x00). 2) Initialise CRC to 0xFFFF. 3) Process each byte with reflected poly 0x8005. 4) Resulting CRC after all bytes is 0xA1B2 (example value). 5) Append CRC low‑order byte first: B2 A1. 6) Frame with flags: 7E FF 03 21 45 00 B2 A1 7E.

quiz.q: A point‑to‑point link is configured in Normal Response Mode (NRM) but both ends start transmitting I‑frames at the same time. What problem arises and how does HDLC recover from it?
quiz.a: Both ends assume they are the primary and send I‑frames without having received the SABM/UA handshake. This leads to frame collisions and loss of synchronization; the receivers will detect FCS errors and discard the frames. HDLC recovers by the primary re‑issuing a Set‑Asynchronous‑Balanced‑Mode (SABM) frame. The secondary responds with an Unnumbered Acknowledgement (UA). After this handshake the link returns to the normal ABM state and I‑frames can be exchanged safely.

beyond: Not for the exam. In modern carrier networks HDLC and PPP are being replaced by Ethernet‑based link layers, but many legacy DSL and satellite modems still use PPP over serial links. Research continues on lightweight framing for IoT devices where code size matters; see work on SLIP and its variants. For deeper study, explore RFC 1661 (PPP) and the ITU‑T recommendation X.25 for historical context. Searching "PPP LCP options" or "HDLC extended mode performance" will reveal recent performance analyses.
